title: Bow, Handshake, Whistle
bigQuestion: How do different rooms show that a fair match has begun?

story.title: Two Rooms, One Minute
story.kicker: At nine o'clock, two classes start in two different ways.
paragraphs: It is nine o'clock at a school in Illinois. In the big gym, a PE teacher lifts a silver whistle. She blows it once. Thirty children stop and turn to face her.
Down the hall is a small room with a soft mat. A judo club meets there. The students stand in a line. They bow to the teacher, and the teacher bows back.
Nobody in either room says, "We are starting now." Still, everyone knows. In one room, the sign is a sound. In the other room, the sign is a bow.

Rooms all over the world have signs like these. A bell rings in boxing. Fencers raise their blades to each other. Wrestlers shake hands. Each sign says the same thing: the match is fair, and it starts now.
story.think: What sign tells your class that it is time to begin?

lessons.title: The Bow in Judo
lessons.mainIdea: In judo, players bow at the start and the end of a match.
reading: Judo began in Tokyo, Japan, in 1882. Its first school was the Kodokan. Its founder was Kanō Jigorō. In judo, the bow is called *rei*. Players bow before a match. They bow again after it ends.
In Japan, a bow is an everyday greeting. People bow to say hello and thank you. In judo, a bow means respect for the other player. After the bow, the referee says *hajime*. That word means "begin."

words.d: the Japanese word for a bow; judo players bow at the start and end of a match
a Japanese word that means begin; the judo referee says it to start a match

The judo referee says hajime to start a match. It means begin.

choices: at the start and end of a match
check.why: Judo players bow before a match and again after it ends.

lessons.title: The Dojo Room
lessons.mainIdea: Many students bow when they walk into a dojo and when they leave it.
reading: A *dojo* is a room for a Japanese art. Judo and karate use dojos. The word means "place of the way." In many dojos, students bow at the door. They bow when they come in and when they go out.
The bow is a greeting and a thank-you. It is not a prayer. People of many religions study judo and karate. Some have no religion at all. Each dojo sets its own customs.

words.d: a room for studying a Japanese art such as judo or karate; the word means place of the way

lessons.title: The Boxing Bell
lessons.mainIdea: In boxing, a bell starts and ends each round.
reading: A boxing match is cut into parts called *rounds*. In 1867, the Queensberry Rules set each round at three minutes. They set a one-minute rest between rounds. Many boxing matches still use these times.
A *bell* rings to start each round. It rings again to end it. The referee calls the two boxers to the middle first. Often the boxers touch gloves. That is a way to say, "Let's have a fair match."

words.d: one part of a boxing match; the Queensberry Rules made each round three minutes
the sound that starts and ends each round in boxing

lessons.title: A Handshake and a Whistle
lessons.mainIdea: In school wrestling, wrestlers shake hands, and a referee's whistle starts the match.
reading: School wrestling in the United States starts with a handshake. The two wrestlers shake hands first. The *referee* blows a whistle to start. A match has three periods of two minutes each.
At the end, the wrestlers shake hands again. Then the referee raises the winner's hand. In Illinois, the IHSA runs school wrestling. The IHSA began in 1900.

words.d: the person who runs a match and makes sure the rules are kept
a greeting where two people hold hands for a moment; wrestlers shake hands before and after a match

lessons.title: Salt in the Sumo Ring
lessons.mainIdea: Before a sumo bout, wrestlers toss salt into the ring to make it clean.
reading: Sumo comes from Japan. Before a bout, many wrestlers toss a handful of *salt* into the ring. The custom comes from *Shinto*. Shinto is an old religion of Japan. In Shinto, salt stands for making a place clean.

A referee called the *gyoji* stands in the ring. He wears bright silk robes. He holds a wooden fan. The two wrestlers start at the same moment, when both are ready. The gyoji points his fan at the winner.

words.d: an old religion of Japan; the salt custom in sumo comes from it
the referee in sumo; he wears silk robes and holds a wooden fan

lessons.title: The Fencer's Salute
lessons.mainIdea: Fencers salute each other before a bout and shake hands after it.
reading: In fencing, a bout starts with a *salute*. Each fencer raises the blade toward the other. They salute the referee too. The world rules for fencing ask for this salute.

Then the referee speaks *French*. The world fencing group began in Paris. First comes "En garde." Next comes "Prêts?" That means "Ready?" Then comes "Allez!" That means "Go!" After the bout, the fencers shake hands.

words.d: a sign of respect; fencers raise their blades to each other before a bout
the language of France; fencing referees use French words to start a bout
